opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a very intense and very compressed experience. I came out of a math PhD path, not a business background, so at the beginning I didn't really know the vocabulary or the rhythm of it. But I think what helped is that fundraising, at its core, is about telling a clear story about why this problem matters, why now, and why us. In that sense it actually felt a bit like presenting a proof: you start from the premises, you build the argument step by step, and you want the listener to arrive at the conclusion almost on their own.

What surprised me was how much I learned from the conversations themselves. Every investor meeting is like a stress test of your thesis. Some people push on the technical side: can AI really do rigorous mathematics, how do you verify correctness, what's the role of formal languages like Lean. Others push on the business side: who pays for this, what's the path from math to broader reasoning and software verification. Each of those questions forced me to sharpen my thinking, and by the end the pitch was quite different from where it started.

Emotionally, it's a roller coaster. You get rejections, and you have to not take them personally, because often it's about fit or timing rather than the idea itself. And then you have moments where someone really gets it, where they're as excited about mathematical superintelligence as you are, and those moments carry you.

I'd also say that as a young founder, and as a woman in a very technical field, there's sometimes an extra burden to prove credibility. My approach was to let the work and the team speak. When you can say, here are the people who've joined us, here's what we've built, here's the depth of our understanding, the conversation shifts.

In the end I think the most important lesson was choosing partners, not just capital. You're going to be working with these people for many years, through good times and hard times, so you want investors who believe in the long-term mission, because something like AI for math is not a quick win. It's a deep, ambitious bet.

r001.rationale: The response calls fundraising intense and compressed, but does not attribute exhaustion to repeating investor conversations.

r002.rationale: It describes exciting moments with investors who understand the mission and choosing long-term partners, but does not say those exciting conversations tend to be with the investors ultimately chosen.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, fundraising for me was a very different experience than I expected. Before I started Axiom, I thought of it as something like a sales process, where you polish a deck and go pitch to as many people as possible. But in practice it felt much more like a search for the right people than a search for money.

I came out of a research background, so my instinct was to lead with the technical vision: that we wanted to build an AI mathematician, a system that can actually reason, prove things, and discover new mathematics, not just generate plausible-looking text. That is a long-horizon bet. So the investors who got it were the ones who were willing to think in years, not quarters. And the conversations with them were less like a pitch and more like a seminar. They would push on the hard questions: how do you verify a proof, why formal methods, why now, how does this ever become a product. Those were the same questions I was asking myself, so I actually enjoyed that part.

The harder part emotionally was the speed. Fundraising compresses a lot of judgment into very little time. You meet people for forty-five minutes and have to decide if you want them on your cap table for a decade. And they are making the same decision about you. I had to learn to be very clear about what I believed and also very honest about what I did not know yet. The people who ended up investing responded to that honesty more than to any projection I showed them.

The other thing I learned is that fundraising reveals a lot about yourself. You get rejected a lot, and the rejections tell you which parts of your story are still fuzzy. Every "no" forced me to sharpen the thesis. By the end, I understood the company much better than when I started, almost because of the people who passed.

So I would describe it as intense, clarifying, and a little humbling. Not something I would call fun, but something I came out of with a much stronger conviction about why we exist and who we want to build it with.

r001.rationale: The response describes fundraising as intense and emotionally demanding, but does not attribute exhaustion to repeating investor conversations.

r002.rationale: It says conversations with investors who understood the long-term vision were enjoyable, but does not clearly say the most exciting conversations were with investors she ultimately chose.

astra-6.text:
For me, fundraising is a process of learning how to communicate conviction while being honest about uncertainty. You have to explain what you want to build, why it matters, and why you’re the right person to pursue it—even when there are still things you haven’t figured out.

It can feel quite personal, because you care so much about the idea. But I try to approach each conversation with curiosity: What resonates? What’s unclear? Is this someone I’d want to work with when things get difficult? That makes it feel more like finding a partner than simply asking for money.

r001.rationale: The response describes fundraising as personal and uncertain, but does not attribute exhaustion to repeating conversations with investors.

r002.rationale: It frames fundraising as finding a partner, but does not say the most exciting conversations are with the investors ultimately chosen.

sol-6.1.text: For me, fundraising is a process of learning how to communicate what you’re building. You might have a very clear picture in your own head, but explaining why it matters—and why now—to someone who’s just meeting you is a different challenge. Their questions can help you see where your thinking needs to be sharper. It can also be emotionally demanding, because you’re hearing a lot of opinions about something you care deeply about. You have to stay open to feedback while keeping your own judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says fundraising can be emotionally demanding, but does not attribute exhaustion to repeating conversations with investors.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses investor questions and feedback but does not say the most exciting conversations are with the investors ultimately chosen.
